title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents

paper.title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents

sections.heading: 1  Introduction
sections.text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that execute multi-step workflows rather than produce isolated responses ( Hsu et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Dong et al., 2026 ) . Each step appends system instructions, skills, earlier decisions, tool interactions, code, and environmental feedback to the next model call. The resulting context connects decisions across time, so losing an early constraint or observation can trigger an inconsistent action whose effects propagate through the remaining trajectory. Preserving the full context, however, increases prefill and attention computation, enlarges the key–value (KV) cache, and forces relevant evidence to compete with stale or redundant information. Long-horizon agents therefore face the central challenge of controlling this growing cost without disrupting the cross-step information flow required for coherent decisions. Reducing context under this constraint is not an ordinary summarization problem. Agent context mixes semantic content with exact values. Explanations, code, and repeated observations can become redundant once the acting LLM has integrated their information, whereas identifiers, API arguments, and numerical values may determine later actions and must remain exact. Information that has little effect on the current action may also become decisive several steps later. Such delayed relevance makes one-shot importance estimates unreliable. Compressibility therefore cannot be inferred from length, repetition, or semantic similarity alone. It depends on what the acting LLM has already absorbed, what the current decision requires, and what a future step may need to recover. Because compression recurs as the trajectory grows, each operation must save more computation than it consumes. Effective context compression must therefore compact information already absorbed by the acting LLM, preserve exact or potentially useful evidence as the task evolves, and deliver savings across subsequent decoding and agent steps. Existing context-compression methods typically rely on training, using either hard-token or soft-token compression. Hard-token methods prune or rewrite text, risking irreversible loss of exact values ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2024a ; Kang et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026b ) . Soft-token methods preserve continuous representations but require separately trained encoders or compressors ( Mu et al., 2023 ; Chevalier et al., 2023 ; Ge et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . More fundamentally, separately trained compressors create a model-taste gap . The information they learn to preserve may not match what the acting LLM has already absorbed or will need later. This motivates an in-model approach that uses the acting LLM’s recurrent state to determine compressibility and carries absorbed information forward as agentic soft tokens. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC) , a training-free approach that uses the acting LLM’s own computation to decide what its growing context must retain. The early layers have read the full context and the later layers would otherwise continue to process every original token. Figure places this boundary within a continuing agent workflow and shows how the choice of compression stage changes task accuracy and workload. In hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)–attention models ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , ASTC examines native recurrent updates and checks whether the retained state can recover a token’s contribution. It keeps exact values explicit as hard tokens and carries eligible content forward as agentic soft tokens. The shorter sequence reduces attention work for the current prediction and creates smaller KV caches that remain reusable as the agent continues. Each compression decision is therefore informed by what the model has already absorbed, and its benefit extends across the trajectory. Across diverse long-horizon tasks, ASTC maintains task quality close to or above the uncompressed model while reducing end-to-end Attention Pairs by up to 50.68%. Preserving exact values avoids the sharp accuracy loss seen when protection is removed, while the compact cache continues to save attention work over later decisions with only small changes in action distributions. The same training-free criterion extends beyond tool observations, matching uncompressed accuracy with 24.52% fewer Decode KV interactions under full-history compression and reducing workload in additional long-context and code-repair tasks. ASTC combines the highest task accuracy with the lowest Attention Pairs per successful task, a 15.4 × \times –103.7 × \times advantage over trained compressors. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify the core challenge of long-horizon compression as reducing context cost without losing future-relevant evidence or diverging from the acting LLM’s task representation. • We introduce ASTC, a training-free method that uses native recurrent dynamics to retain exact values as hard tokens and carry absorbed content forward as soft tokens with reusable compact KV caches across subsequent agent steps. • We bound trained-compressor objective mismatch, establish conditions under which ASTC has lower next-token distortion than equal-length hard-token representations, and quantify attention savings from cache reuse. • Across long-horizon tasks, ASTC achieves comparable or better accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs and a 15.4 × \times –103.7 × \times advantage in end-to-end Attention Pairs per successful task over trained compressors.

sections.heading: 2.1  In-Model Soft Tokens
sections.text: Context compression determines both how many tokens remain and which evidence reaches the acting LLM. Existing methods make this decision before the model processes the compressed context, either pruning tokens or rewriting earlier interactions as shorter text ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ; Kang et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026b ) . This ordering creates a selection mismatch because the value of a context span is not intrinsic to its text. It depends on how the acting LLM represents the current task, what it has already absorbed, and which action it is about to take; the same observation can be redundant at one step and decisive at another. An external compressor must approximate this model-dependent boundary from text alone. In a long-horizon trajectory, a mistaken deletion can propagate because later decisions are made from the retained context.Hard-token output adds a second bottleneck because retained information must be serialized as a shorter sequence of vocabulary tokens, so exact structure or features distributed across positions must be reconstructed as short text. Even a correctly selected span can therefore lose task-relevant information when forced into a short textual rewrite. Moving compression inside the model lets the acting LLM judge compressibility where task information is represented, while soft tokens retain information in continuous contextual representations. In-model selection and soft-token representation are therefore complementary, letting the acting LLM judge what matters and preserve that information in its own representation space, thereby avoiding both external selection mismatch and discrete textual reconstruction.

sections.heading: 2.2  Tool Observations
sections.text: Figure 1: Composition of accumulated context in real-world agent trajectories. We analyze agent trajectories from real-world user interactions across systems such as Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.2 ( Anthropic, 2026 ; OpenAI, 2026 ; Moonshot AI, 2026 ; Z.AI, 2026 ) . As Figure 1 shows, a consistent pattern emerges across these trajectories. Tool observations occupy the largest share of the accumulated context and continue to grow as the agent interacts with its environment. In our experiments, tool observations are the primary compression target. Tool observations are difficult to compress because they mix compressible natural-language and code spans with exact values, such as paths, identifiers, and checksums, that later actions may consume verbatim. Our preliminary experiments show that the former tolerates aggressive compression, whereas changing a single character in the latter can invalidate a later action. This heterogeneity makes tool observations a demanding but informative testbed. Effective agent compression must therefore compact semantic information distributed across many tokens without altering the exact values on which future actions depend.

sections.heading: 2.3  Model-Native Selection
sections.text: Our initial approach followed existing work by training a separate in-model compressor to produce soft tokens. We inserted an attention–MLP compressor after either a single backbone layer or multiple layers, thereby compressing the hidden sequence once or repeatedly, and trained it with On-policy distillation (OPD) . Comparing these variants with ACON and LCLM reveals a consistent pattern: training-based compression incurs substantial preparation cost yet delivers weak task performance, while repeated intervention across more layers offers no remedy (Figure ) ( Kang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . This failure reflects a difficult optimization problem. An auxiliary compressor must infer what the acting LLM has already absorbed, retain information that later steps may require, and emit features compatible with downstream layers, all through an objective separate from the LLM’s native prediction process. Hybrid GDN–attention models already compute a signal closely aligned with this decision during their normal forward pass. A GDN recurrent state acts as an online associative memory. Its gated delta update can be written as ( Yang et al., 2025 ) 𝐒 t = α t ​ 𝐒 t − 1 + β t ​ 𝐫 t ​ 𝐤 t ⊤ , 𝐫 t = 𝐯 t − α t ​ 𝐒 t − 1 ​ 𝐤 t , \mathbf{S}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{S}_{t-1}+\beta_{t}\mathbf{r}_{t}\mathbf{k}_{t}^{\top},\qquad\mathbf{r}_{t}=\mathbf{v}_{t}-\alpha_{t}\mathbf{S}_{t-1}\mathbf{k}_{t}, (1) where α t \alpha_{t} controls how much previous memory survives, β t \beta_{t} controls the write strength, and 𝐫 t \mathbf{r}_{t} is the part of the incoming value that cannot be recovered from the retained state. Information already represented by the state produces a small correction, whereas novel or conflicting information changes the memory more strongly. The update therefore measures information relative to what the acting LLM currently remembers, not importance inferred from surface form alone. Moreover, the gate and delta update are optimized jointly with the LLM’s predictions, so this distinction shares the representation space and task state used by downstream layers. Reusing GDN dynamics avoids teaching an auxiliary compressor to approximate the acting LLM’s own notion of novelty. Training-free selection is therefore not merely a cheaper alternative; it follows from recognizing that the acting LLM has already performed the information judgment that compression requires.

sections.heading: 3  Related Work
sections.text: Discrete context compression shortens the sequence before it reaches the acting LLM. Selective Context ( Li et al., 2023 ) prunes redundant spans; LLMLingua ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) and LongLLMLingua ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) rank tokens for prompt pruning; LLMLingua-2 ( Pan et al., 2024 ) learns selection from distilled labels; and RECOMP ( Xu et al., 2024a ) trains compressors for retrieved evidence. For extended agent workflows, ACON ( Kang et al., 2026 ) optimizes textual compression guidelines from task failures, while Context as a Tool (CAT) ( Liu et al., 2026b ) trains SWE-Compressor to invoke context management during execution. MEM1 ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) instead trains a compact memory jointly with agent reasoning. While these lines reduce accumulated context, text-level selection can discard exact evidence or diverge from the acting LLM’s evolving task representation, and learned memory policies require additional training. Meta Context Engineering ( Ye et al., 2026 ) co-evolves agentic skills and context artifacts to optimize task-specific context construction. Soft-token methods retain information in continuous states. Gist Tokens ( Mu et al., 2023 ) learns compressed prompt activations, AutoCompressors ( Chevalier et al., 2023 ) produce recursive summary vectors, and ICAE ( Ge et al., 2024 ) trains compact memory slots. Sentinel Tokens ( Ren et al., 2023 ) and Activation Beacon ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) compress intermediate activations for later processing. DAST ( Chen et al., 2025 ) allocates soft tokens according to contextual information density, while Latent Context Language Models (LCLMs) ( Li et al., 2026 ) train dedicated encoder–decoder models for large-scale compression. For tool-using LMs, Xu et al. (2024b) combine compressed representations with raw tokens for exact tool interfaces. These studies show that continuous memory can support incremental reuse and coexist with exact-token retention. Their compression behavior is nevertheless learned through model adaptation or auxiliary components, and their primary settings differ from a growing history of agent actions and observations. KV-cache eviction offers another route: H 2 O ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) retains recent and heavy-hitter tokens, while SnapKV ( Li et al., 2024 ) selects important positions per attention head. Archer ( He et al., 2026 ) adapts prompt-K/V reuse to evolving response states in rollback-capable diffusion language models. ASTC brings the continuous memory studied in soft-token compression to the growing histories addressed by agent context-management work. By operating within the acting LLM without a separately trained compressor, it keeps compression tied to the model’s evolving task representation. To the best of our knowledge, ASTC is among the first in-model soft-token methods designed for context compression in long-horizon LLM agents. sections.heading: 5  Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate ASTC with a frozen Qwen3.5-9B acting model on AppWorld ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ) , OfficeBench ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , and 8-Objective QA ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Kang et al., 2026 ) . We compare with uncompressed Base, prompted compression, LLMLingua ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) , LLMLingua-2 ( Pan et al., 2024 ) , ACON UT and UTCO ( Kang et al., 2026 ) , and LCLM ( Li et al., 2026 ) . In Table 1 , ASTC compresses only eligible tool observations. We measure task quality and end-to-end Decode KV, Attention Pairs, and Generated Tokens. Decode KV counts decoding query–cache interactions; Attention Pairs counts causal query–key pairs across prefill, decoding, and auxiliary calls. Supplementary analyses and detailed setups are in Appendices C – I .

sections.heading: 5.2  Model-Native Selector Controls
sections.text: We ask whether ASTC’s GDN signals improve selection beyond what protection and sequence shortening provide. We test this by retaining the acting model, protection rules, and legal group construction while changing the selection rule. Hidden-only uses hidden-state reconstruction error to test whether local fidelity suffices; Random assigns fixed random scores to test whether protected grouping alone explains the gains. Each policy runs the full AppWorld in closed loop, allowing compression choices to shape later actions, tool observations, and workload. Figure 3 compares task success with end-to-end Attention Pairs and shows ASTC’s strongest joint outcome, consistent with the value of model-native selection. Because trajectories and compression events differ, the comparison evaluates complete policies; paired bootstrap uncertainty makes the success advantage suggestive rather than conclusive. The comparison suggests that the acting model’s accumulated state supplies information about compressibility beyond local reconstruction (Appendix G ). Figure 3: Selector controls on AppWorld.

sections.heading: 5.3  Persistence After One Commit
sections.text: Compression helps a long-horizon agent only if its shorter KV cache remains useful when later steps revisit it, without substantially changing the agent’s decisions. To isolate this mechanism, we branch from archived Base trajectories, allow at most one ASTC commit in one branch, and replay identical subsequent action tokens and tool results in both. This fixed continuation separates the effect of persistent cache compression from changes caused by diverging actions or observations. With no further commits allowed, savings at later horizons reflect reuse of the initial cache update rather than repeated compression. At successive action horizons during the shared continuation, we measure KL divergence between conditional action-token distributions and cumulative Attention Pairs saved since the commit. Figure 4 shows that the distributions remain close while savings recur at later actions, supporting the proposed amortization across the trajectory. A separate autonomous one-commit run probes whether this local stability carries through to task outcomes; its success is somewhat lower than archived Base and full ASTC, and differing archive versions make the comparison descriptive. Appendix H reports all replayed actions and a fixed task cohort, showing how savings accumulate as the compact cache is reused. Figure 4: One-commit cache reuse and task outcomes. Middle: cumulative Attention Pairs saved since the commit; the observed task set varies across horizons.

sections.heading: 6  Conclusion
sections.text: Long-horizon agents must retain evidence for future decisions as context grows, while separately trained compressors may drift from the acting LLM’s evolving task representation. ASTC uses native recurrent dynamics after early layers have read the full sequence, carrying absorbed content as agentic soft tokens and keeping exact values as hard tokens. The shorter sequence cuts later-layer computation and creates a compact KV cache whose savings persist across subsequent decisions. Without compressor training, ASTC keeps accuracy close to or above the uncompressed agent with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs; in the controlled comparison, it attains the highest accuracy and lowest Attention Pairs per successful task. Ablations and fixed-continuation analysis link these gains to exact-value protection, model-native selection, and persistent cache reuse. These results show how the acting LLM can compact absorbed context into reusable state without losing exact evidence for later decisions.

The separate whole-task one-commit policy succeeds on 49/168 tasks, compared descriptively with 54/168 archived Base and 56/168 released ASTC. Released ASTC may commit once for each new observation, rather than once for the entire task. First-commit action, R R , and generated token IDs agree with released ASTC on all 160 triggered tasks, but 10 of 37 comparable source files differ between archives. These scores therefore do not identify a same-code causal effect of allowing later commits. They also do not turn fixed-input fidelity into an autonomous success or noninferiority guarantee. Uncertainty and scope. New overall fidelity and final savings intervals use 10,000 percentile task-bootstrap resamples, NumPy default_rng seed 20261019. The fixed cohort is exploratory; no multiple-comparison correction is applied. Replay measures prediction fidelity on stored inputs, not retrieval accuracy for facts available only in merged observations.

sections.heading: I.1  General Setup
sections.text: Benchmarks. We evaluate ASTC on three long-horizon agentic benchmarks with distinct interaction structures. AppWorld provides a simulated ecosystem of everyday applications and APIs for interactive coding agents; we use its full 168-task Test-Normal split ( Trivedi et al., 2024 ) . OfficeBench covers realistic office-automation workflows that require planning, application switching, and grounded actions across productivity software ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . 8-Objective QA groups eight Natural Questions into each task and requires an agent to gather evidence with a Wikipedia search tool before returning all eight answers ( Kwiatkowski et al., 2019 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Kang et al., 2026 ) . Together, they test compression across API interaction, office automation, and multi-question information gathering. Implementation. The three main benchmarks use the frozen Qwen3.5-9B acting model. For Table 1 , all methods within each benchmark share the acting-model serving configuration and evaluation protocol. Base and ASTC also share the agent scaffold, prompts, decoding policy, context limit, and action budget. Model checkpoints. The main experiments use Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B at Hugging Face revision c202236235762e1c871ad0ccb60c8ee5ba337b9a ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) . The transfer study also uses moonshotai/Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct at revision e1df551a447157d4658b573f9a695d57658590e9 ( Moonshot AI, 2025 ) . The cross-model study in Section 5.5 also uses the frozen Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B model in BF16. Bounded pooling. Selected positions are divided into at most M M groups in causal order. In each group, an existing member closest to the mean direction anchors an initial trim by relative ℓ 2 \ell_{2} error. ASTC then averages the remaining states in FP32, casts the mean to the runtime dtype, and accepts a group of at least two members only if its maximum post-cast relative error is at most τ h \tau_{h} . Rejected and trimmed positions remain hard tokens. This check bounds hidden-state reconstruction, not downstream attention scores. Baselines. Base is the uncompressed acting LLM. We compare ASTC with representative hard-token approaches, including prompted compression, LLMLingua ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) , LLMLingua-2 ( Pan et al., 2024 ) , and the UT and UTCO variants of ACON ( Kang et al., 2026 ) , as well as LCLM, a trained soft-token compressor ( Li et al., 2026 ) . These external-compressor comparisons are reported on AppWorld and OfficeBench; 8-Objective QA also includes Prompting, both LLMLingua variants, both ACON variants, and LCLM. The newly reported AppWorld LLMLingua-2 and OfficeBench Prompting and LLMLingua runs compress observations; the remaining hard-token baselines compress the full context, whereas ASTC compresses eligible tool observations in-model. All methods that require training use Qwen3.5-9B as the backbone and are evaluated with the same benchmark protocol. End-to-end workload includes acting-model requests, auxiliary compressor-service calls, compressor-generated tokens, and repeated prefills. The 8-Objective QA counts include the LLMLingua v1 and LLMLingua-2 service forwards. Workload metrics. Decode KV counts query–cache interactions during autoregressive decoding. Attention Pairs also includes prefill and auxiliary model calls, while Generated Tokens counts all discrete outputs. These are analytical counts, not measured latency or GPU operations. Each workload metric in Table 1 is normalized to Base within its benchmark. Related context and cache optimization. Meta Context Engineering (MCE) co-evolves agentic skills and context artifacts for task-specific context construction ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . Archer reuses prompt K/V while recomputing mutable responses in rollback-capable diffusion language models ( He et al., 2026 ) . These works address context construction and rollback-aware caching, respectively, while ASTC focuses on in-model compression and persistent cache reuse along agent trajectories.

sections.heading: I.2  Benchmark-Specific Configurations
sections.text: For the three main benchmarks in Table 1 , we follow the benchmark tasks, agent scaffolds, model-serving settings, inference limits, and evaluation procedures of ACON ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . The benchmark settings and ASTC-specific compression policies are detailed below. AppWorld. We evaluate all 168 AppWorld 0.1.3.post1 Test-Normal tasks under this ACON-aligned setup. The frozen Qwen3.5-9B agent uses greedy decoding, at most 50 actions, 768 output tokens per action, and a 32,768-token logical context. The model seed is 20260914, and task i i uses seed 20260912 + i 20260912+i in the released task order. ASTC operates after zero-based GDN layer 10 and before attention layer 11, retaining at most 16 soft tokens per tool observation. Its fixed reader is calibrated from 22 records across 12 Train/Dev tasks, without weight updates. Each head uses leading eigenvectors of trace-normalized tool-end state covariances; the ridge and RMS stabilizers are λ = 10 − 4 \lambda=10^{-4} and ϵ = 10 − 6 \epsilon=10^{-6} . The ordinary-data thresholds are χ < 0.60 \chi<0.60 , ψ < 0.80 \psi<0.80 , and merge error ≤ 0.50 \leq 0.50 ; the conservative catalog thresholds are 0.55 0.55 , 0.74 0.74 , and 0.55 0.55 , respectively. A commit must save at least 256 downstream token-layer positions and 5% of eligible tool positions. API contracts, catalogs, and exact-value fields are protected. OfficeBench. We use the official Test split, Qwen3.5-9B, seed 20260920, and the official environment and evaluator. The agent uses at most 50 iterations, 768 output tokens per action, and a 32,768-token context. OfficeBench uses the same ASTC layer, selection thresholds, merge bound, and persistent cache as AppWorld. Only later byte-identical repetitions of an application-interface scaffold are eligible for compression; the first copy, changed scaffolds, observations, task instructions, system text, and prior actions remain explicit. Base and ASTC share the prompt and action budget. 8-Objective QA. All methods evaluate the same ACON Test tasks. The frozen Qwen3.5-9B acting model uses BF16 with vLLM 0.18.0, a 131,072-token model limit, engine seed 42, and at most 30 agent iterations for every method. ASTC compresses eligible tool content at the AppWorld layer boundary; the reported policy uses ( χ , ψ ) = ( 0.55 , 0.75 ) (\chi,\psi)=(0.55,0.75) for ordinary tool data. EM and F1 score the eight answers per task. All methods share the same serving and evaluation configuration, and workload is normalized to the corresponding Base run.

sections.heading: I.3  Additional-Dataset Protocols
sections.text: RULER. We evaluate the same 32K inputs in Base and ASTC with the frozen Qwen3.5-9B model and a 32,768-token context limit. RULER scores answers by task-specific string matching and averages over its 13 task configurations. We use 20 examples per task, rather than the reference configuration’s 500. Thus the reported accuracy is a 260-example aggregate; matching aggregate scores do not imply identical results on every task or at the larger default sample size. ASTC uses the Stage-3 data branch with ( χ , ψ ) = ( 0.60 , 0.80 ) (\chi,\psi)=(0.60,0.80) and merge-error threshold 0.50 0.50 . Decode KV and Attention Pairs are analytical query–cache and causal-pair counts; Gen. is generated tokens, all normalized to Base. LongBench v2. We use all 503 four-choice questions in the public train split ( Bai et al., 2024 ) . Base and ASTC share the frozen Qwen3.5-9B model and a 262,144-token context limit; examples that exceed the limit are truncated before either method processes them. Of the 503 examples, 100 require truncation. The inference configuration permits at most 16 new tokens; the recorded runs generate two tokens per example in both variants. ASTC uses the Stage-3 catalog branch with ( χ , ψ ) = ( 0.55 , 0.74 ) (\chi,\psi)=(0.55,0.74) , merge-error threshold 0.55 0.55 , and minimum net removal of one token. Overall and subgroup accuracy are exact-match rates for the extracted choice. Reported KV counts and cache bytes are analytical logical workload measures, not latency or measured peak device memory. For MBPP, we use the sanitized task snapshot from Archer ( He et al., 2026 ) . MBPP. We use its 427 sanitized MBPP problems ( Austin et al., 2021 ) . This interactive code-repair protocol is not numerically comparable with one-shot MBPP evaluations. The model submits a complete Python program, receives public-test feedback, and revises it; a third attempt is allowed if the second fails. The final program is scored once. Both variants use greedy decoding, at most 768 generated tokens per attempt, and a 32,768-token context limit. ASTC uses its Stage-3 calibration, thresholds, and 16-soft-token bound. Initial prompts, completed code, and public-test feedback are eligible for compression, while special control tokens remain explicit. Both variants re-prefill the full transcript before each turn; workload includes these repeated prefills and all decoding calls.

However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM’s evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC) , a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model’s native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)–attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent’s trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent’s accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 15.4 × \times –103.7 × \times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves. GitHub Repo: https://github.com/RISE-X-Lab/Agentic-Soft-Token Correspondence: dongyh@sjtu.edu.cn 0 0 footnotetext: 🖂: Corresponding author. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that execute multi-step workflows rather than produce isolated responses ( Hsu et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Dong et al., 2026 ) . Each step appends system instructions, skills, earlier decisions, tool interactions, code, and environmental feedback to the next model call. The resulting context connects decisions across time, so losing an early constraint or observation can trigger an inconsistent action whose effects propagate through the remaining trajectory. Preserving the full context, however, increases prefill and attention computation, enlarges the key–value (KV) cache, and forces relevant evidence to compete with stale or redundant information. Long-horizon agents therefore face the central challenge of controlling this growing cost without disrupting the cross-step information flow required for coherent decisions. Reducing context under this constraint is not an ordinary summarization problem. Agent context mixes semantic content with exact values. Explanations, code, and repeated observations can become redundant once the acting LLM has integrated their information, whereas identifiers, API arguments, and numerical values may determine later actions and must remain exact. Information that has little effect on the current action may also become decisive several steps later. Such delayed relevance makes one-shot importance estimates unreliable. Compressibility therefore cannot be inferred from length, repetition, or semantic similarity alone. It depends on what the acting LLM has already absorbed, what the current decision requires, and what a future step may need to recover. Because compression recurs as the trajectory grows, each operation must save more computation than it consumes. Effective context compression must therefore compact information already absorbed by the acting LLM, preserve exact or potentially useful evidence as the task evolves, and deliver savings across subsequent decoding and agent steps. Existing context-compression methods typically rely on training, using either hard-token or soft-token compression. Hard-token methods prune or rewrite text, risking irreversible loss of exact values ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2024a ; Kang et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026b ) . Soft-token methods preserve continuous representations but require separately trained encoders or compressors ( Mu et al., 2023 ; Chevalier et al., 2023 ; Ge et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . More fundamentally, separately trained compressors create a model-taste gap . The information they learn to preserve may not match what the acting LLM has already absorbed or will need later. This motivates an in-model approach that uses the acting LLM’s recurrent state to determine compressibility and carries absorbed information forward as agentic soft tokens. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC) , a training-free approach that uses the acting LLM’s own computation to decide what its growing context must retain. The early layers have read the full context and the later layers would otherwise continue to process every original token. Figure places this boundary within a continuing agent workflow and shows how the choice of compression stage changes task accuracy and workload. In hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)–attention models ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , ASTC examines native recurrent updates and checks whether the retained state can recover a token’s contribution. It keeps exact values explicit as hard tokens and carries eligible content forward as agentic soft tokens. The shorter sequence reduces attention work for the current prediction and creates smaller KV caches that remain reusable as the agent continues. Each compression decision is therefore informed by what the model has already absorbed, and its benefit extends across the trajectory. Across diverse long-horizon tasks, ASTC maintains task quality close to or above the uncompressed model while reducing end-to-end Attention Pairs by up to 50.68%. Preserving exact values avoids the sharp accuracy loss seen when protection is removed, while the compact cache continues to save attention work over later decisions with only small changes in action distributions. The same training-free criterion extends beyond tool observations, matching uncompressed accuracy with 24.52% fewer Decode KV interactions under full-history compression and reducing workload in additional long-context and code-repair tasks. ASTC combines the highest task accuracy with the lowest Attention Pairs per successful task, a 15.4 × \times –103.7 × \times advantage over trained compressors. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify the core challenge of long-horizon compression as reducing context cost without losing future-relevant evidence or diverging from the acting LLM’s task representation. • We introduce ASTC, a training-free method that uses native recurrent dynamics to retain exact values as hard tokens and carry absorbed content forward as soft tokens with reusable compact KV caches across subsequent agent steps. • We bound trained-compressor objective mismatch, establish conditions under which ASTC has lower next-token distortion than equal-length hard-token representations, and quantify attention savings from cache reuse. • Across long-horizon tasks, ASTC achieves comparable or better accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs and a 15.4 × \times –103.7 × \times advantage in end-to-end Attention Pairs per successful task over trained compressors. 2 Motivation 2.1 In-Model Soft Tokens Context compression determines both how many tokens remain and which evidence reaches the acting LLM. Existing methods make this decision before the model processes the compressed context, either pruning tokens or rewriting earlier interactions as shorter text ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ; Kang et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026b ) . This ordering creates a selection mismatch because the value of a context span is not intrinsic to its text. It depends on how the acting LLM represents the current task, what it has already absorbed, and which action it is about to take; the same observation can be redundant at one step and decisive at another. An external compressor must approximate this model-dependent boundary from text alone. In a long-horizon trajectory, a mistaken deletion can propagate because later decisions are made from the retained context.Hard-token output adds a second bottleneck because retained information must be serialized as a shorter sequence of vocabulary tokens, so exact structure or features distributed across positions must be reconstructed as short text. Even a correctly selected span can therefore lose task-relevant information when forced into a short textual rewrite. Moving compression inside the model lets the acting LLM judge compressibility where task information is represented, while soft tokens retain information in continuous contextual representations. In-model selection and soft-token representation are therefore complementary, letting the acting LLM judge what matters and preserve that information in its own representation space, thereby avoiding both external selection mismatch and discrete textual reconstruction. 2.2 Tool Observations Figure 1: Composition of accumulated context in real-world agent trajectories. We analyze agent trajectories from real-world user interactions across systems such as Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.2 ( Anthropic, 2026 ; OpenAI, 2026 ; Moonshot AI, 2026 ; Z.AI, 2026 ) . As Figure 1 shows, a consistent pattern emerges across these trajectories. Tool observations occupy the largest share of the accumulated context and continue to grow as the agent interacts with its environment. In our experiments, tool observations are the primary compression target. Tool observations are difficult to compress because they mix compressible natural-language and code spans with exact values, such as paths, identifiers, and checksums, that later actions may consume verbatim. Our preliminary experiments show that the former tolerates aggressive compression, whereas changing a single character in the latter can invalidate a later action. This heterogeneity makes tool observations a demanding but informative testbed. Effective agent compression must therefore compact semantic information distributed across many tokens without altering the exact values on which future actions depend. 2.3 Model-Native Selection Our initial approach followed existing work by training a separate in-model compressor to produce soft tokens. We inserted an attention–MLP compressor after either a single backbone layer or multiple layers, thereby compressing the hidden sequence once or repeatedly, and trained it with On-policy distillation (OPD) . Comparing these variants with ACON and LCLM reveals a consistent pattern: training-based compression incurs substantial preparation cost yet delivers weak task performance, while repeated intervention across more layers offers no remedy (Figure ) ( Kang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . This failure reflects a difficult optimization problem. An auxiliary compressor must infer what the acting LLM has already absorbed, retain information that later steps may require, and emit features compatible with downstream layers, all through an objective separate from the LLM’s native prediction process. Hybrid GDN–attention models already compute a signal closely aligned with this decision during their normal forward pass. A GDN recurrent state acts as an online associative memory. Its gated delta update can be written as ( Yang et al., 2025 ) 𝐒 t = α t ​ 𝐒 t − 1 + β t ​ 𝐫 t ​ 𝐤 t ⊤ , 𝐫 t = 𝐯 t − α t ​ 𝐒 t − 1 ​ 𝐤 t , \mathbf{S}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{S}_{t-1}+\beta_{t}\mathbf{r}_{t}\mathbf{k}_{t}^{\top},\qquad\mathbf{r}_{t}=\mathbf{v}_{t}-\alpha_{t}\mathbf{S}_{t-1}\mathbf{k}_{t}, (1) where α t \alpha_{t} controls how much previous memory survives, β t \beta_{t} controls the write strength, and 𝐫 t \mathbf{r}_{t} is the part of the incoming value that cannot be recovered from the retained state. Information already represented by the state produces a small correction, whereas novel or conflicting information changes the memory more strongly. The update therefore measures information relative to what the acting LLM currently remembers, not importance inferred from surface form alone. Moreover, the gate and delta update are optimized jointly with the LLM’s predictions, so this distinction shares the representation space and task state used by downstream layers. Reusing GDN dynamics avoids teaching an auxiliary compressor to approximate the acting LLM’s own notion of novelty. Training-free selection is therefore not merely a cheaper alternative; it follows from recognizing that the acting LLM has already performed the information judgment that compression requires. 3 Related Work Discrete context compression shortens the sequence before it reaches the acting LLM. Selective Context ( Li et al., 2023 ) prunes redundant spans; LLMLingua ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) and LongLLMLingua ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) rank tokens for prompt pruning; LLMLingua-2 ( Pan et al., 2024 ) learns selection from distilled labels; and RECOMP ( Xu et al., 2024a ) trains compressors for retrieved evidence. For extended agent workflows, ACON ( Kang et al., 2026 ) optimizes textual compression guidelines from task failures, while Context as a Tool (CAT) ( Liu et al., 2026b ) trains SWE-Compressor to invoke context management during execution. MEM1 ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) instead trains a compact memory jointly with agent reasoning. While these lines reduce accumulated context, text-level selection can discard exact evidence or diverge from the acting LLM’s evolving task representation, and learned memory policies require additional training. Meta Context Engineering ( Ye et al., 2026 ) co-evolves agentic skills and context artifacts to optimize task-specific context construction. Soft-token methods retain information in continuous states. Gist Tokens ( Mu et al., 2023 ) learns compressed prompt activations, AutoCompressors ( Chevalier et al., 2023 ) produce recursive summary vectors, and ICAE ( Ge et al., 2024 ) trains compact memory slots. Sentinel Tokens ( Ren et al., 2023 ) and Activation Beacon ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) compress intermediate activations for later processing. DAST ( Chen et al., 2025 ) allocates soft tokens according to contextual information density, while Latent Context Language Models (LCLMs) ( Li et al., 2026 ) train dedicated encoder–decoder models for large-scale compression. For tool-using LMs, Xu et al. (2024b) combine compressed representations with raw tokens for exact tool interfaces. These studies show that continuous memory can support incremental reuse and coexist with exact-token retention. Their compression behavior is nevertheless learned through model adaptation or auxiliary components, and their primary settings differ from a growing history of agent actions and observations. KV-cache eviction offers another route: H 2 O ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) retains recent and heavy-hitter tokens, while SnapKV ( Li et al., 2024 ) selects important positions per attention head. Archer ( He et al., 2026 ) adapts prompt-K/V reuse to evolving response states in rollback-capable diffusion language models. ASTC brings the continuous memory studied in soft-token compression to the growing histories addressed by agent context-management work. By operating within the acting LLM without a separately trained compressor, it keeps compression tied to the model’s evolving task representation. To the best of our knowledge, ASTC is among the first in-model soft-token methods designed for context compression in long-horizon LLM agents. ASTC uses native recurrent dynamics after early layers have read the full sequence, carrying absorbed content as agentic soft tokens and keeping exact values as hard tokens. The shorter sequence cuts later-layer computation and creates a compact KV cache whose savings persist across subsequent decisions. Without compressor training, ASTC keeps accuracy close to or above the uncompressed agent with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs; in the controlled comparison, it attains the highest accuracy and lowest Attention Pairs per successful task. Ablations and fixed-continuation analysis link these gains to exact-value protection, model-native selection, and persistent cache reuse. These results show how the acting LLM can compact absorbed context into reusable state without losing exact evidence for later decisions.
